content:
I just reviewed a PR (#40877) which was adding a lemma not_prime_four.

We already have prime_two, prime_three, and prime_five, so this is consistent with the existing code. But it is this really "Right Thing"?

It seems to me that this is the sort of thing that should be handled by automation, rather than hard-coded lemmas. Sadly, example : Nat.Prime 5 := by norm_num doesn't work (nor does simp or grind); the only tactic which does work here is decide. What do we consider the "morally sound" way of dealing with these very simple goals?

(In fact the documentation for norm_num claims "It also has a relatively simple primality prover", but it apparently doesn't work at the moment [EDIT: it doesn't work if it's not imported!].)

It's possible that you're just missing an import, this works on live.lean-lang.org:

import Mathlib

example : ¬ Nat.Prime 4 := by norm_num
example : Nat.Prime 5 := by norm_num

norm_num does work for this, just not in that file, since the primality prover extension is in a later file (Mathlib/Tactic/NormNum/Prime.lean). In application, norm_num is currently the best thing Mathlib provides.
Presumably the docstring should mention that import Mathlib.Tactic.NormNum.Prime is required.

Oh I have also been caught by this! The general phenomenon seems to be that (a) norm_num is an extensible tactic (b) the extensions are not imported by default so (c) you can see norm_num failing to prove things which it can prove.

David Loeffler said:

I just reviewed a PR (#40877) which was adding a lemma not_prime_four.

I'm working on refactoring arguments where I can use not_prime_XXX more than prime_YYY. It might be good to analyze that part of Mathlib that uses one or the other (or both) types. After this refactor, I plan to re-examine the arguments to see if they apply to more rings which have the same not_primes, and generalize accordingly. Perhaps something can be done for the 'not_prime' portions of Mathlib.

content: After finding out how they are used, it might be useful to collect all the facts into a single module so that the usage of norm_num for these facts is localized, or the generation of the facts is systematized.

content: The real question is whether it can prove 57 is prime.
I suspect Ryan Smith is making a reference to the Grothendieck prime

J. J. Issai (project started by GRP) said:

After finding out how they are used, it might be useful to collect all the facts into a single module so that the usage of norm_num for these facts is localized, or the generation of the facts is systematized.

I actually think we should do precisely the opposite: we should always use norm_num for primality proving outside a few foundational files.
I have made a PR #41186 which clarifies the docstrings of norm_num, to remind users that they need an extra import to access the primality prover.
